clue.text: Make six deliveries, and impress greatly

blocks.note: the cricket sense: a bowler's turn of six balls

explanation.walkthrough: The deliveries are cricket balls, not parcels: in cricket an over is six balls, all sent down by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, six deliveries are what a bowler sends down in an over; figuratively, to be bowled over is to be knocked flat with admiration.

clue.text: Clog dance

blocks.note: a verb here: to clump up and block, as wet snow does in a horse's hooves
a formal evening of dancing, as in Cinderella

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one thing, a clog dance, but splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Two unrelated senses: a verb for gathering into lumps that choke something, and a noun for a grand formal dance.

clue.text: Bridge player, working at large shop, mostly, wanting kip in coastal resort

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter
a word wanting something lacks it, so that letter comes out

blocks.note: the four bridge players are named North, South, East and West
a machine that is working is on
K is the abbreviation for the kip, the currency of Laos

explanation.surface: A card player who works in a big store needs a nap on a seaside holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Kip is British slang for sleep, which is how the surface wants it read; here it is the Laotian currency. The shop loses its last letter and then its K.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the town is a Victorian seaside resort on the Somerset coast of the Bristol Channel.

clue.text: Pop-up books about United's rival

indicators.note: things that are stirred up are thrown out of order
the jumbled letters go round about the next piece

blocks.note: NT = New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
people who are united are at one

explanation.surface: A children's pop-up book about Manchester United's great rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop-up books' looks like a single noun, a children's book with fold-out pictures; the hyphen hides that 'up' is an instruction and 'books' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rival is whoever you are competing against.

clue.text: Kick out six in English court

blocks.note: CT = court, as in street names

explanation.surface: Six people are thrown out of an English court.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's word order is six, English, court, but 'in' puts six between English and court.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a landlord kicking out a tenant is the everyday sense.

clue.text: Noticed hosts beginning to cook with seasoning

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the word holds the letter within it
the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to spy something is to catch sight of it

explanation.surface: Someone spots a host starting to cook a seasoned dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hosts' reads as dinner-party hosts, fitting the cooking; here it is only a container.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase and the adjective both describe food flavoured with spices, so they swap in 'a dish ___'.

clue.text: Maybe Afghan father shot crook

indicators.note: as an adjective crook means bent, and the letters are bent out of shape

explanation.surface: An Afghan's father may have shot a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crook' looks like a noun for a criminal; here it is an adjective, and 'Maybe' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Afghan can name a language of Afghanistan, and this is one of its two official languages, alongside Dari.

clue.text: Emperor let her gate-crash parties

indicators.note: as a verb, to party is to go wild, and wild letters do not keep their order

explanation.surface: An emperor allows a woman to crash his parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parties' reads as the noun, the parties she crashes; here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is Charlemagne, crowned Emperor of the Romans in the year 800.

clue.text: Deprive of claim in Settle, strangely, after I'd turned up

indicators.note: letters behaving strangely are out of their usual order
in a down clue, turning up flips the letters to read from the bottom
the anagram comes after the flipped piece

explanation.surface: Someone loses a claim in the town of Settle after oddly turning up there.
explanation.walkthrough: Settle is a market town in North Yorkshire, and its capital letter hides that the word is just anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The prefix dis- undoes entitle, which means to give a claim, so the verb means to take that claim away.

clue.text: Joke beer bottles getting one complaint

indicators.note: as a verb, to bottle something is to shut it inside

blocks.note: to rib someone is to tease or joke with them

explanation.surface: A joke about someone drinking bottles of beer and ending up with a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' reads as a noun for beer bottles; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint in the medical sense, an ailment: this is a disease caused by lack of vitamin B1.

clue.text: Suggested cost of lean rump, finally, with side dish

indicators.note: the final part of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a ship that lists leans to one side
a common accompaniment to a main course

explanation.surface: A diner asks the price of a lean rump steak served with a side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' reads as an adjective for meat; here it is the verb, to tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: The retail term for the price a maker recommends, before any discount a shop may give.

clue.text: Marks vehicles on style, at first

indicators.note: what comes at first in a word is its first letter
in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it

explanation.surface: A judge scores vehicles on style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' reads as a verb for grading; here it is the noun, blemishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: marks left on skin or a surface after damage.

clue.text: Relative wasting American's money

indicators.note: something wasting away is losing part of itself

explanation.surface: A relative squanders an American's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasting' reads as squandering money; here it means wasting away, losing letters from the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass noun for metal money, as in 'paid in ___'.

clue.text: Experiment with running over most of the competition

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter
one piece laid over another covers it on both sides

blocks.note: a show that is running is on

explanation.surface: Someone experiments with running for most of a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: The running of the surface really belongs in the answer's scene, which is the misdirection: it only supplies two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a race of swimming, cycling and running.

clue.text: Bishop can start to disregard rule in place for fox hunting?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
one piece goes in another

blocks.note: can and loo are both slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A bishop might ignore a ban at the place where fox hunting goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: Can is American slang for a toilet, as loo is British slang. The question mark marks fox hunting as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: fox hunting, banned in Britain in 2005, is the classic case of a sport in which animals are killed.

clue.text: Alleges son destroyed city

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, and its letters can be put back any way

explanation.surface: A parent claims their son wrecked a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Son' wants to be the usual S, but the whole word is needed in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Californian city, the second largest in the United States.

clue.text: What keeps still, extremely withdrawn? A canine offered in swap deal?

definitions.text: A canine offered in swap deal?

indicators.note: whatever keeps something holds it inside
a withdrawn army goes back the way it came, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: eh? and what? both ask someone to repeat themselves
still and yet both mean up to now

explanation.surface: Two riddles: what stays still and very withdrawn, and which dog is offered in a trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine' wants to be a dog; it is a tooth. The swap deal is the old law of revenge, 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint: the upper canine is called by this name, and both of its halves are offered in the eye-for-an-eye, tooth-for-a-tooth trade.

clue.text: Sex appeals after knocking back wine

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it back the way it came

blocks.note: IT and SA are both slang for sex appeal, so the plural needs two of them

explanation.surface: Someone becomes attractive after downing some wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocking back' is drinking in the surface, which is why the wine seems to be what gets swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sparkling white wine from Piedmont in Italy.

clue.text: Welsh town boosted politician in Europe with no money

indicators.note: in a down clue, boosting a word lifts it so it reads upward

blocks.note: MEP = Member of the European Parliament
someone with no money is broke

explanation.surface: A Welsh town gets a lift from a penniless Euro-politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boosted' reads as helped or promoted; its job is a direction, upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a castle town in south-west Wales that gives its name to Pembrokeshire.

clue.text: I've made a mistake over love note at end of e-mail, perhaps

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

blocks.clueFragment: note at end of e-mail, perhaps
blocks.note: PS = postscript, a note added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone regrets a love note tacked on to the end of an email.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole spoken sentence, and a single exclamation can stand in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is exactly what people say to admit a small blunder.

clue.text: Content to pass Emile thalidomide — it's fairly harmful to genes

indicators.note: the answer is the content held within the next words

explanation.surface: A warning about giving thalidomide to someone called Emile, since it can harm unborn children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy to; here it means the contents of the following words. Thalidomide was a 1950s drug that caused birth defects, which makes the surface grimly apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A genetics term: semi- means half, so the gene kills some but not all of the organisms that carry it.

clue.text: Manipulates desires in audition

indicators.note: an audition is literally a hearing, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a word for wants or requirements

explanation.surface: A director gets their way with actors at a tryout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audition' looks like a casting session; here it means hearing, and the silent K is what the spelling adds.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the physical sense: working dough or muscles with the hands.

clue.text: Active nurses out dancing

indicators.note: dancers move about, and so do the letters

explanation.surface: Energetic nurses on a night out dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the night out, but it is fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an active or strenuous day is one full of vigorous effort.

clue.text: Is back for one last bit of private investment

indicators.note: going back means reading backwards
the last bit of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A last small private investment comes back to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The financial surface hides an old military word.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: to invest a town is to surround it with troops, so investment is the act of besieging.

clue.text: Annoys German boarding aircraft

indicators.note: a passenger boarding a vehicle goes inside it

blocks.note: bus is pilots' slang for an aircraft

explanation.surface: A German passenger irritates people while getting on a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: The vehicle is an aircraft in the surface, but the letters come from the pilots' nickname for it, which is the everyday word for a road vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain informal synonym: to irritate or pester.

clue.text: Boss in workplace having ten leaving

indicators.note: the letters leave, so they drop out of the word

blocks.note: ten written as the figures 1 and 0, which look like IO

explanation.surface: A boss's workplace loses ten staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' reads as a manager; here it is a boss in the sense of a raised knob.
explanation.definitionFit: A less common sense: a boss is a round knob standing out from a surface, as on a shield or a belt.

clue.text: Rejected a ham omelette, initially, in Nebraskan city

indicators.note: what comes initially in a word is its first letter
a rejected dish is sent back, so the letters go back

blocks.note: taken as written. The same letters also run on unbroken across neighbouring clue words, a coincidence of the pieces sitting side by side; the setter gives no hidden-word signal.

explanation.surface: A diner in Nebraska sends back a ham omelette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' works in the surface as sending food back and in the wordplay as turning the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the largest city in the US state of Nebraska.

clue.text: Fresh article covering popular water sports venue

indicators.note: one worker covering for another takes their place

explanation.surface: A new magazine piece about a popular place for sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' looks like new, for the article; here it is the cheeky sense. The Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the strait hosts Cowes Week and much of Britain's yachting.

clue.text: Belief system is welcomed by those people

indicators.note: a guest welcomed by a host is taken inside

explanation.surface: A set of beliefs finds a welcome among a group.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'is' before 'welcomed' is both fodder and part of the indicator phrase in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: belief in a god who created and rules the world.

clue.text: Conquered one achievement, inspiring another

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, taking something inside

blocks.note: an act, especially a notable one
a second word for an achievement

explanation.surface: Having conquered, one success leads to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' reads as encouraging; its literal Latin sense, breathing in, is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: beaten in battle or a contest.
